are also sent to the voice as its direction (never spoken aloud). The dialogue is Shakespeare's, untouched (it comes from the cue sheets);
this file adds the scene headings, the action and blocking, and parentheticals.
Keys: 'voice' (where the scene is played — SENT TO THE VOICE with every spoken line, 9 Oct 2026), 'slug' (scene heading), 'open' (action before the first line), 'before' {cue n: [action

1.slug: EXT. ROME — A STREET NEAR THE FORUM — DAY
1.voice: Outdoors on a crowded, noisy holiday street: a raised, projected voice that carries over the crowd
open: February, 44 BC. The Feast of Lupercal. Garlands hang from the statues; the shops are shuttered for the holiday.
A THRONG OF CITIZENS pours down the street toward the Forum — tradesmen in their best tunics, laughing, shoving, a few waving sprigs of laurel for Caesar.
Laughter, shouting, whistling — a holiday crowd in full cry.

Hooves on the stones. Two TRIBUNES ride into the crowd and rein in hard: FLAVIUS, hard and quick, and MARULLUS, older, colder. The horses snort and stamp, pacing back and forth. The purple stripe on their togas stops the crowd dead.

5: A broad-shouldered CARPENTER is shoved to the front by the men behind him.
7: Beside him, a wiry COBBLER with a grin that has never once been respectful. He plays to the crowd behind him.
13: The crowd laughs. Marullus does not.
18: Marullus mounts the base of a statue so the whole street can see him.
19: The crowd has gone quiet, shamed. Caps come off.
21: The crowd melts away; the shuffling and the noise die to nothing. Flavius and Marullus are left alone among the garlands.
23: Flavius reaches up and tears a wreath from a statue of Caesar. He drops it in the dust, wheels his horse and rides down the street, overturning the stalls; his shouts carry back over Marullus.

paren.4: from the saddle — angry, scolding, condescending; the questions sharp and badgering
paren.18: sharp, exasperated — let each question hang

2.slug: EXT. ROME — THE VIA SACRA, A PUBLIC PLACE — DAY
2.voice: Outdoors in a public street during a procession, music and crowds nearby: a projected voice; quieter and closer when two speak apart
open: Flutes and drums. The PROCESSION fills the street: lictors with their rods, then CAESAR in a purple toga and a laurel wreath, borne along on the roar of the crowd.

Beside him CALPURNIA, his wife, veiled. MARK ANTONY, stripped to a goatskin for the sacred race, bouncing on his toes. Behind them the great men of Rome: DECIUS, CICERO, CASCA — and, a little apart from the rest, BRUTUS and CASSIUS.
Somewhere in the press, an old SOOTHSAYER pushes forward.

3: Caesar raises a hand. The procession halts.
8: Calpurnia steps to the edge of the course. Antony grins at her.
14: A thin cry cuts through the music. Heads turn.
18: The crowd parts. The SOOTHSAYER stands alone in the open street — blind, ragged, utterly still.
23: Cassius takes the old man by the arm and leads him to Caesar. Caesar studies his face for a long moment.
26: Caesar laughs it off. The procession moves on.
28: The street empties around BRUTUS and CASSIUS. Far off, the roar of the games.
32: Cassius moves closer. They walk together, slowly, under the colonnade.
40: Brutus stops dead, looking toward the noise.
46: Cassius drops his voice. Brutus does not look at him.
50: The procession returns. Caesar walks fast, his face set. Calpurnia pale. The others follow in an uneasy silence.
54: Caesar stops — and looks straight at Cassius across the street. Then he beckons Antony close.
60: CASCA lingers, then ambles over, brushing at the sleeve Brutus pulled.
76: Casca mimes it — the fall, the foaming mouth — enjoying himself.
95: Casca saunters off, whistling. Brutus watches him go.
100: Cassius alone. The cheerful mask drops from his face.

3.voice: Outdoors at night in a violent thunderstorm: voices raised over wind, rain and thunder
open: The night before the Ides of March. A storm the city will talk about for a hundred years.

Lightning splits the sky. Rain sheets across the paving. CASCA comes running down the empty street, sword drawn, soaked and wild-eyed — and almost collides with CICERO, wrapped in his cloak, walking home as if nothing were the matter.

6: Thunder. Casca grips Cicero’s arm; his words tumble out.
11: Cicero pulls his cloak tight and goes. Casca is alone in the storm.
12: A figure strides out of the rain: CASSIUS, bareheaded, his cloak open to the lightning.
19: Cassius throws his arms wide to the storm.
25: Cassius draws a dagger and holds it up in the lightning.
31: Footsteps. Both men shrink back into a doorway. CINNA hurries past — then stops, peering at them.
39: Cassius pulls out a packet of papers, sealed, and presses them into Cinna’s hands.
43: Cinna runs off into the rain. Cassius turns to Casca with a fierce smile.

4.voice: Outdoors at night in a quiet walled garden, the storm passing: low, private voices, close and unhurried
open: The small hours before the Ides. Wind in the fig trees; the last of the storm grumbling far off. A lamp in the doorway of the house.
BRUTUS walks the paths alone, cloak loose, unable to sleep. He calls into the dark for his boy.

10: Brutus stops beneath a tree. He speaks to no one.
24: A knock at the gate. Brutus does not move.
37: Hooded men slip in through the gate, faces buried in their cloaks.
81: The conspirators melt into the dark. The garden is still again.
84: PORTIA in the doorway, barefoot, a shawl around her shoulders.
91: She kneels on the wet stones. He lifts her.

5.voice: Indoors in a great house at dawn, thunder still rolling outside: voices in a large stone room, intimate but strained
open: Thunder over the roofs. Grey light through high windows. CAESAR in his nightgown, sleepless, restless as a caged lion.
Somewhere in the house a servant hurries away with an order for the priests.

9: CALPURNIA comes in fast, hair unbound, white with fear from her dream.
30: DECIUS, smiling, steps between husband and wife.
34: The conspirators arrive in their best togas, smiling, to escort Caesar to the Senate.

6.slug: EXT. ROME — A STREET NEAR THE CAPITOL — MORNING
6.voice: Outdoors on a busy morning street: a single man reading half-aloud to himself, urgent and low
open: The Ides of March. Crowds already gathering toward the Capitol. ARTEMIDORUS, an old teacher, stands in a doorway reading his own letter over and over.

7.slug: EXT. ROME — BEFORE BRUTUS’S HOUSE — MORNING
7.voice: Outdoors in a doorway on a noisy morning street: an anxious woman, breathless, voice catching
open: PORTIA paces the threshold of her house, sending her boy LUCIUS to the Capitol and calling him back before he reaches the gate.

13: The old SOOTHSAYER shuffles past, toward the Capitol.

8.slug: INT. ROME — THE SENATE, BEFORE THE CAPITOL — DAY
8.voice: In a great stone senate hall echoing with voices: formal, public, every word carrying
open: The Ides of March. Trumpets. CAESAR sweeps up the steps through the crowd, senators in his wake. The SOOTHSAYER waits on the steps.
Inside, the marble hall: tiers of senators, the statue of Pompey watching over all.

43: The petitioners close around Caesar. CASCA strikes first; then all the knives.
44: Caesar sees BRUTUS among them. He stops fighting.
45: Caesar falls at the foot of Pompey’s statue. Silence — then the hall erupts.
68: The conspirators stand over the body, hands red.
78: ANTONY enters, sees the body, and goes to it before he sees anyone else.

9.voice: Outdoors in the vast Roman Forum before a huge restless crowd: projected voices that carry across the square
open: The Forum, packed to the colonnades. BRUTUS mounts the speakers’ platform. Below, Caesar’s body is carried in under a bloody mantle.

12: ANTONY walks behind the bier, slow, head bowed.
65: Antony comes down from the platform and stands among the crowd, at the body.
72: The crowd turns. Torches. The Forum becomes a mob.

10.voice: Outdoors in a street overrun by a torch-lit mob: shouting, menacing voices over the noise
open: Smoke and torchlight. CINNA THE POET, a gentle man in a scholar’s cloak, wanders out of his house, troubled by a dream — into the mob.

11.slug: INT. ROME — A ROOM IN ANTONY’S HOUSE — NIGHT
11.voice: Indoors, a private room at night: three men at a table, low, businesslike voices
open: Lamplight on a table covered with lists. ANTONY, OCTAVIUS and LEPIDUS sit pricking names — the men who will die.

12: Lepidus leaves. Antony waits until the door closes.

12.slug: EXT. CAMP NEAR SARDIS — BEFORE BRUTUS’S TENT — DUSK
12.voice: Outdoors in an army camp at dusk, soldiers about: clipped military voices
open: Campfires coming alight across the hills. Drums. BRUTUS stands before his tent as a messenger rides in from Cassius.

16: CASSIUS marches in with his men, angry before he has said a word.

13.voice: Inside a soldier’s tent at night: close, private voices; the anger kept low so the camp will not hear
open: A lamp, a table of maps, a cot. The tent flap drops. BRUTUS and CASSIUS face each other alone.

82: The quarrel spent. LUCIUS brings wine; they drink together.
148: Lucius takes up his lute. The music slows; the boy’s head drops. Brutus reads by the taper.
150: The taper gutters. A shape stands at the tent’s mouth: CAESAR, as he died.

14.slug: EXT. THE PLAINS OF PHILIPPI — DAY
14.voice: Outdoors on an open plain, two armies drawn up: commanders shouting across open ground, wind carrying the words
open: A wide plain under a hard sky. Two armies face each other. The four generals ride out to parley in the middle ground.

39: The parley breaks. Brutus and Cassius are left alone in the wind.

15.slug: EXT. PHILIPPI — THE FIELD OF BATTLE — DAY
15.voice: Outdoors in the middle of a battle: shouted orders over the noise
open: Dust and noise. BRUTUS gallops up with a handful of written orders.

16.slug: EXT. PHILIPPI — A HILL ON THE FIELD — DAY
16.voice: Outdoors on a hilltop above a battle: urgent voices, the fighting below
open: A rise of ground. CASSIUS, his standard-bearer fled, his tents on fire, watches the field with TITINIUS.

13: PINDARUS climbs to the crest to look.
20: A shout from below — Titinius among horsemen. Cassius misreads it.
28: TITINIUS returns, a wreath of victory in his hand — too late.

17.slug: EXT. PHILIPPI — ANOTHER PART OF THE FIELD — DAY
17.voice: Outdoors in the thick of a battle: young men shouting their names in defiance
open: Hand to hand. Young CATO and LUCILIUS fight back to back.

16: ANTONY rides up as Lucilius is dragged before him.

18.slug: EXT. PHILIPPI — A ROCK ON THE FIELD — EVENING
18.voice: Outdoors at evening as a lost battle fades: tired, close voices among a few men
open: The battle lost. A rock at the edge of the field. BRUTUS and the last of his friends rest in the failing light.

36: Strato holds the sword. Brutus runs upon it.
37: The victors arrive. ANTONY stands over the body.
